account: Boston Children’s Hospital and OpenAI researchers used o3 Deep Research to reassess 376 rare-disease cases that remained unresolved in their local research records. They reported 18 confirmed local diagnoses, or 4.8%: 11 newly identified diagnoses and seven rediscoveries of diagnoses already made elsewhere. Clinicians reviewed candidates, arranged laboratory confirmation, and returned results to families. The paper’s discussion explains that some findings depended on later gene discoveries, revised classifications, previously uncalled variants, or information that was unavailable to earlier analyses. The researchers did not compare the model with a simultaneous expert reanalysis using the same current evidence. They also did not measure improvements in treatment, cost, or clinician time. NBC News separately interviewed Kyra Benton about receiving a diagnosis and sought comment from outside clinicians. The study was retrospective and involved OpenAI employees and funding, so it does not establish an independent estimate of the model’s added benefit.

ai_role.statement: o3 Deep Research read each de-identified case packet and proposed the most plausible molecular explanation with its supporting evidence. It diagnosed no one. Humans did the rest. At least two reviewers adjudicated each candidate under ACMG/AMP criteria, a CLIA-certified laboratory confirmed each variant, and the clinical team returned results to families. Its distinct contribution was surfacing candidates in cases that commercial and institutional analyses and multidisciplinary teams had already reviewed. In one early-psychosis case it inferred a 22q11.2 deletion absent from the input data, which genome sequencing then confirmed. Seven of the 18 were rediscoveries already established externally. The study was retrospective, and reviewers were not blinded to model confidence. The authors call for prospective evaluation with comparator baselines, so the gain over renewed human reanalysis is unmeasured.

fields.account: Boston Children’s Hospital and OpenAI researchers used o3 Deep Research to reassess 376 rare-disease cases that remained unresolved in their local research records. They reported 18 confirmed local diagnoses, or 4.8%: 11 newly identified diagnoses and seven rediscoveries of diagnoses already made elsewhere. Clinicians reviewed candidates, arranged laboratory confirmation, and returned results to families. The paper’s discussion explains that some findings depended on later gene discoveries, revised classifications, previously uncalled variants, or information that was unavailable to earlier analyses. The researchers did not compare the model with a simultaneous expert reanalysis using the same current evidence. They also did not measure improvements in treatment, cost, or clinician time. NBC News separately interviewed Kyra Benton about receiving a diagnosis and sought comment from outside clinicians. The study was retrospective and involved OpenAI employees and funding, so it does not establish an independent estimate of the model’s added benefit.
